where.label: supported
where.says: Sitges is a town about 35 km southwest of Barcelona, between the Garraf Massif and the Mediterranean, known for its film festival, Carnival, beaches and LGBTQ+ tourism.
quote: is a town about 35 kilometres southwest of Barcelona, in Catalonia, Spain, renowned worldwide for its film festival, Carnival, and Catalan culture. Located between the Garraf Massif and the Mediterranean Sea, it is known for its beaches, nightspots, LGBTQ+ tourism, and historical sites.

name.label: supported
name.says: The name is the Catalan word for silos or granaries; the old town center was probably built around the castle where the silos stood.
quote: The name of the town is simply the Catalan word sitges, plural of sitja, meaning 'silos', cisterns or granaries in English.
it is assumed that the original town center was built around the castle (the area of today's town hall) precisely where these storage structures were situated.

quote: Between the late-18th century and the early-20th, the history of Sitges was dominated by its close links with Spain's overseas territories, most importantly Cuba. Thousands of youngsters from Sitges settled in Santiago de Cuba, Guantánamo and other areas in Eastern Cuba.
Some of them thrived and created big firms, like Facundo Bacardí, founder of Ron Bacardí

quote: These were known as "Americanos", known for their habit of planting palm trees in their Caribbean-looking houses, smoking Cuban cigars and rum drinking. The americanos left a huge legacy in Sitges which can still be seen in its architecture

quote: The first beach bar in Spain opened in Sitges in 1913, called El Kiosket and renamed in 1949 "chiringuito" by the Spanish journalist César González Ruano, inspired by his experiences travelling Cuba where coffee was strained through a stocking called "chiringo".
it has created the name of every beach bar  in Spain "Chiringuito"

quote: For over a century, Sitges has celebrated Carnestoltes, or Carnival
The festivities begin on Dijous Gras, or Fat Thursday, with King Carnestoltes' arrival. They continue until the burial of the sardine — late afternoon on Ash Wednesday.
Around forty floats with more than 2,000 participants fill Sitges.

malvasia.label: supported
malvasia.says: Malvasia, a sweet wine served with dessert, takes its name from the Greek port of Monemvasía; the Hospital Sant Joan Baptista still makes it, about 4,000 bottles a year, for charity.
quote: Malvasia is a delicate liquor wine served in Sitges, primarily with dessert. The name "malvasia" comes from the Peloponnesian port Monemvasía. In Sitges, the Hospital Sant Joan Baptista continues producing and marketing malvasia according to the traditional method from its own vines and within its own cellars. The proceeds go to charity. The annual production is approximately 4,000 bottles.

parts.name: The seafront
parts.stand: On the Passeig de la Ribera, the seafront promenade, looking toward the old church above the promenade.

paras.t: Welcome to Sitges, about 35 kilometers southwest of Barcelona, squeezed between the Garraf hills and the Mediterranean. It's famous for its beaches, its film festival, its Carnival, and for welcoming LGBTQ+ visitors. That's the old church up there, above the promenade.
On a sunny day the light off the sea is strong. Wear a hat, drink water, and find some shade now and then.

The name is humble. Sitges simply means silos, or granaries, in Catalan, and the first town probably grew up around the castle where they stood. The story goes that the Romans called it Blanca subur, the white town.

People have been here a very long time. Neanderthal bones and stone tools turned up in a cave near today's golf course, La Cova del Gegant, showing people in Sitges at least 50,000 years ago. And in 1958 this quiet resort even made history far away: Colombia's rival Liberal and Conservative leaders met here and signed a peace treaty, the Declaration of Sitges.
There are 17 beaches in Sitges, so if this one's crowded, keep walking.

parts.name: The Cuba connection
parts.stand: Turn your back to the sea and look into the town.

paras.t: For over a century, this little town looked across the Atlantic. Thousands of young people from Sitges went to eastern Cuba. Some made fortunes there. One of them, Facundo Bacardí, founded Bacardí rum.
Those who came home rich were called the Americanos. They liked to plant palm trees by their Caribbean-looking houses, and you can still see their legacy in the town's buildings.

Here's a fun one. Spain's first beach bar opened here in 1913, called El Kiosket. In 1949 a journalist renamed it the chiringuito, after a cloth coffee strainer he'd seen in Cuba called a chiringo. Every beach bar in Spain is now a chiringuito.
Sitges made shoes, too. The first mechanized shoe factory in Spain opened here in 1874. It was tourism, booming in the 1960s, that finally ended the shoe-making era.

parts.name: The painter's house
parts.stand: Outside the Cau Ferrat Museum in the old town.

paras.t: This is the Cau Ferrat, once the studio of Santiago Rusiñol, painter, writer and one of the leaders of Catalan modernisme. He set up here in 1893, and Sitges became a magnet for artists, writers and musicians, with festivals mixing theater, poetry, painting and music.
Inside, look for a small Picasso and several paintings by El Greco, alongside works by Catalan modernists.

After the artists came the money. Wealthy Barcelona families built summer houses here, and the town became known abroad. The American collector Charles Deering kept his art in Sitges from 1910 to 1921, and built the Palau Maricel.

The party never really stopped. The film festival, devoted to fantasy and horror, has been held every October since 1968. And Carnival, celebrated for over a century, runs from Fat Thursday to the burial of the sardine on Ash Wednesday, with around forty floats and more than 2,000 people in the parades.

parts.name: A glass of malvasia
parts.stand: Back by the sea, wherever you'd like to sit for a moment.

paras.t: Before you leave, try the local malvasia, a sweet wine served with dessert. The name comes from Monemvasía, a port in Greece's Peloponnese. Here in Sitges an old hospital still makes it from its own vines, about 4,000 bottles a year, and the money goes to charity.
Young people left this town for Cuba, and came home with palm trees. A painter came and set up his studio. Sitges has always been a place people arrive at and make their own. Maybe you will too.
